transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-08-21 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Jamie Torres (Redwood AE), Evan Park (Redwood SE), Sana Rizvi (HelioMed ML Eng), Tom Becker (HelioMed Platform Eng), Lena Ortiz (Head of Data)

Summary: quick follow-up on last week's incidents (timeouts and 5xxs) observed in the pilot. Walked through traces Jamie exported, clarified rate-limit behavior, agreed tentative retry/backoff change and actions to run a targeted benchmark and escalate quota.

Topics: incident triage, 429/5xx patterns, client retry policy, KV/prefix cache impacts, canary fallback, monitoring/alerts, next steps

Questions: who owns the client library in HelioMed? (Sana), what percent of calls are >512 tokens? (Sana to measure)

[00:00] Jamie: Okay, thanks everyone for carving out time. Quick agenda — triage the reliability blips you saw Mon/Tue, look at the traces you sent, and agree next steps. I'm Jamie, AE. Evan will go into the traces.
[00:18] Evan: Hi all. I pulled three example traces you included in the packet — the ones with the 500s and the 429s. My first pass, I see a cluster of 5xx that line up with sudden spikes in seq length and a bursty ingress pattern. There's also a lot of retry churn from the client side.
[00:36] Sana: Yeah that matches what we saw — morning batch job had several long prompt generation paths and we had a throttle pop. We were using the default client retry config, I think 5 retries?
[00:48] Tom: It was the stock library. We haven't tuned it. There was also a platform job that retried a subset of requests concurrently which may have amplified load.
[01:02] Evan: Okay, two quick things — one, those retries without exponential backoff can create retry storms that convert transient 429s into sustained 5xx windows. Two, sequences at the 95th percentile were much longer on the traces, which increases per-token CPU/GPU time.
[01:22] Lena: When you say sequence length, is that including the KV cache warm-up or raw prompt length?
[01:30] Evan: Good Q. The traces show prompt+history — raw tokens. The KV cache warm-up matters for cold starts, but this looks like sustained long sequences during a run. Could be model choice too.
[01:45] Sana: We are testing several open models — some smaller ones for freshness, a Llama2-70 variant for certain prompts. The 5xx spikes happened when we hit a larger model variant for a tranche of requests.
[01:58] Jamie: Right. From Redwood side, we saw a transient elevation in load against your project key when the larger model rolled in. We had autoscaling trying to keep up but the burst was faster than provisioning.
[02:12] Tom: Logs show 429s with headers indicating per-minute quota and also 5xxs with a 'kernel OOM' note for some requests — could be memory pressure on less optimized kernels.
[02:26] Evan: Kernel OOM — yes that can happen when sequence length spikes for certain quantized execution paths. One mitigation is using a lower memory model variant as fallback or enabling continuous KV caching for repeated prefixes to avoid recomputation.
[02:42] Sana: Is there a config we can tweak right away? We need a short-term fix for the pilot while we look at longer-term tuning.
[02:50] Evan: Short term: reduce client retries to 3, add jittered exponential backoff (base 500ms), and limit concurrency from the platform job so it doesn't fan out retries. Also, consider routing large requests to a dedicated worker pool or fallback to a smaller model automatically.
[03:10] Jamie: We'll also temporarily raise burst capacity on your dedicated pool — that requires a quick infra approval but we can do a short-lived bump while you stabilize.
[03:22] Tom: That would help. Is there a risk with making retries fewer? We're worried about losing successful requests.
[03:29] Evan: Fewer retries with exponential backoff is better than many tight retries. The worst offenders are no backoff + many retries. The policy we propose: 3 retries, exponential backoff with jitter, max backoff 3s. That reduces effective pressure and still recovers transient failures.
[03:46] Sana: Sounds reasonable. We'll need a patch to our client lib — we control it. Evan, can you share a concrete snippet?
[03:52] Evan: Yes, I'll push a PR with the config and a small wrapper that respects Retry-After and X-RateLimit headers. Also include logic to avoid retrying on 5xx that are classified as server unrecoverable — we'll list codes in the doc.
[04:10] Lena: About the 5xxs — are they always server-side? Could our input be causing the runtime to hit bad paths?
[04:17] Evan: Sometimes input causes very long decoding loops which can surface as out-of-memory in certain kernel paths. We'll correlate the trace IDs you send to see tokenization patterns. Also check if you have unusually high context window usage.
[04:32] Jamie: Can you confirm how you captured the traces? We need the three trace IDs.
[04:36] Sana: Yes we exported the traces from our app — I'll attach them after. We anonymized user data.
[04:42] Evan: Perfect. Send the trace IDs and I'll map to the request logs and GPU telemetry.
[04:49] [05:00] (brief crosstalk) Tom: We did also see a bunch of 502s around 09:12 UTC — are those consistent with overload?
[05:12] Evan: 502s can be proxy or gateway responses when an upstream worker is unresponsive; if that lines with high queue lengths that's overload.
[05:20] Jamie: Quick status on monitoring/alerts: the alerting thresholds were tripped but some of the flips were noisy. We recommended an additional signal: track request queue latency on each worker and alert on >200ms queue latency for 2x within 5 minutes. That helps catch backpressure earlier.
[05:38] Sana: Good call. We'll add that.
[05:43] Evan: Another immediate knob: enable prefix caching for repeated user prompts — if your workload has repeat prefixes we can cache token outputs and shave a lot off. This requires a config change and some storage for prefix keys.
[05:59] Tom: We have some repeated preambles in the clinical prompts — likely good candidate. Do you have a recommended cache size?
[06:07] Evan: Start small — a 10k entry LRU for the most common prefixes and measure hit rate. We'll suggest a heuristic after we see the initial traces.
[06:18] Lena: On the security/enterprise side — raising burst or changing routing touches our governance. We'll need an approvals note.
[06:26] Jamie: Understood — we'll document the temporary burst bump and the duration, and include audit logs. Also we'll share the security brief you asked for (SOC2 coverage, KMS integration details).
[06:36] Sana: Thanks. Can we make sure the logs we share redact PHI? We already did, but wanted to confirm.
[06:41] Evan: Yes please redact PHI — trace IDs and org-level metadata are sufficient for us to debug.
[06:47] [07:00] (longer pause while notes are taken)
[07:15] Tom: About rate-limit headers — we saw X-RateLimit-Remaining drop to zero then a 429. Is the billing tier tied to that?
[07:25] Jamie: The per-project quota is configurable; for Dedicated you get higher default quotas and we can set burst allowances if committed capacity is in place. We'll surface those numbers in the follow-up.
[07:35] Lena: For the pilot we can't commit more spend yet, but a short-term burst increase would be acceptable.
[07:42] Jamie: We'll propose a 2x temporary burst for 48 hours while we stabilize, and we'll log the change. If you need more, we can look at reserved capacity.
[07:52] Sana: Ok. Next — telemetry: can Redwood provide aggregated 95th/99th per-model latencies so we can map ours?
[07:59] Evan: Yes we can export per-model percentiles and tail latency for the window you care about. I'll attach CSVs.
[08:07] Jamie: Also, we'll give you a small client patch and the recommended retry policy. We'll link a short runbook (https://rwd.co/reliability-playbook) we've been iterating on.
[08:18] Sana: Great, that helps.
[08:22] Evan: One more consideration — if your platform's job fan-out pattern is causing retries to reissue at scale, consider adding a leader-election/coordination so only one process retries a failed logical task. That can dramatically reduce duplicate requests.
[08:39] Tom: We can try a coordinator lock in Redis quickly.
[08:43] Evan: Perfect.
[08:46] Jamie: To summarize the technical fixes: 1) Client retry policy change (3 retries, jittered exp backoff), 2) Limit concurrency on the platform job, 3) Enable prefix caching for common prompts, 4) Temporary burst quota increase, 5) SE to map traces to kernel OOMs and suggest model variant fallback.
[09:07] Lena: That list is good. For governance, we'll need the temporary changes documented.
[09:13] Jamie: We'll email a short change notice and include audit links.
[09:18] Evan: Next on the cadence: we'll reconvene in 1 week after you've run the longer-sequence benchmark and applied the client patch. If problems persist, we'll do a deeper infra postmortem.
[09:29] Sana: Sounds good.
[09:33] Jamie: Any other questions?
[09:36] [09:40] (Sana) — just one: can you share the kernel OOM examples without the full logs?
[09:44] Evan: Yes, anonymized snippets and the telemetry metrics.
[09:48] Tom: I'll also share the platform job config — concurrency, backoff, and retry behavior.
[09:54] Jamie: Great. I'll follow up after this call with the temporary burst change and the proposed retry snippet. Evan will share the PR and per-model latency CSVs.
[10:04] (wrap) Lena: Thanks everyone. Appreciate the quick triage.
[10:08] Jamie: Thanks all — we'll get those items turned around fast.

References/links mentioned: https://rwd.co/reliability-playbook (playbook deck), PR link placeholder to be shared by Evan, redacted logs to be uploaded to shared drive.

End of transcript.
